De Kanesatake à Montréal-Nord, ceux qui: From Kanesatake to Montréal-Nord, Those Living With Bill 96
Arrêtez d’être riche, devenez plus pauvr: Stop being rich, become poorer! It’s crazy, because you would never say that to someone.
Le projet de loi 96, qui est devenu loi: Bill 96, which became law and came into force last June, aims to strengthen the French language in society. Photo: Ramy Berkani
La langue française occupe une place fon: The French language holds a fundamental place in Quebec society. It is the language of culture, politics and everyday life. The French fact in North America is a singularity celebrated by French-speaking Quebecers and by all who cherish diversity. Yet all across Quebec, some people have a less positive relationship with the French language. From Kanesatake to Montréal-Nord, several of them tell us about their relationship with French. Bill 96, which became law and came into force last June, aims to strengthen the French language in society.
À ce titre, cette loi touche de nombreux: As such, the law touches many areas, including health, education and immigration. Among the changes it brings are additional French courses in English-language CEGEPs, a requirement for immigrants to learn French within six months, and the establishment of French as the mandatory language in public services, unless one belongs to a historically English-speaking community.
Hany Shokair, étudiant de l’Université C: Hany Shokair, a Concordia University student and Syrian refugee since 2019. Photo: Fatima Bah
« Six mois, ce n’est pas assez pour appr: “Six months isn’t enough to learn a language. When we talk about a language, we’re talking about a culture, a way of thinking. It’s not just about repeating a word over and over,” says Hany Shokair, a Concordia University student. For him, it was a shock to hear about Section 22 of <l1>Bill 96</l1>. That section requires administrative bodies to serve immigrants exclusively in French once the six-month period following their arrival in Quebec has ended. Hany himself went through this stage of migration after arriving in the province in 2019 as a Syrian refugee.
Il se range derrière plusieurs experts q: He sides with several experts who denounce this section of the law and consider it discriminatory. Seated at a table in his kitchen, the young man describes what he went through during those first months in Quebec and his experience in French classes. As a refugee, he was forced to leave his life, and everything he had built, to come to a country where he had no bearings. The person handling his file enrolled him in francization classes a few weeks after his arrival. For Hany, francization was a very difficult ordeal: “It literally took me two months to understand that ‘a’ and ‘e’ are pronounced differently in French and in English.” In his view, requiring people who are fleeing their country and carrying a painful past to master a new language in six months minimizes their trauma and their past. “When I was at school, my brain was thinking about my problems; I wasn’t in a good state to learn French.” The migration process is in itself a heavy burden that these individuals must overcome while under a great deal of stress.
Pour l’étudiant d’origine syrienne, les: For the student of Syrian origin, francization classes were also one of his only sources of income. “During my six or seven months at school, I wasn’t mentally ready to learn French. I was just afraid that if I missed a class, the government wouldn’t pay me and I wouldn’t be able to pay my rent,” he confides. In his Vieux-Rosemont apartment, which he shares with another international student, the young man continues: “We were learning everything so fast! For example, one week we’d learn verbs in the present tense and the next week we’d learn the past.”
À la fin de ses cours, Hany n’avait pas: By the end of his classes, Hany’s French wasn’t at a good level. After seven months of francization, he was only able to find a job as a grocery store clerk. “Even with my level, my employers didn’t trust me enough to let me work long hours,” explains the graduate in international relations and engineering from Syria and Lebanon.
Faisant face à tant de difficultés dans: Faced with so many difficulties in learning French, Hany decided to turn to McGill University to improve his English. He feels the English-language system is better suited to his reality. “I was in a university system and I had more time to practise, but the most important thing was having mental health support services and counsellors,” says the sexology student at Concordia University, who still continues to practise his French through his volunteer involvement.

Djazia Bousnina, une jeune diplômée en s: Djazia Bousnina, a young political science graduate from Concordia. Photo: Ramy Berkani
Le parcours de Hany Shokair rappelle cel: Hany Shokair’s path is reminiscent of that of Djazia Bousnina, a young Algerian woman who graduated in political science from Concordia.
Assise dans un confortable fauteuil de l: Seated in a comfortable chair in the green space of Parc Pierre-Laporte in Montréal-Nord, Djazia explains her particular relationship with the French language. The young Montrealer emigrated from Algeria about ten years ago with the rest of her family. She speaks fluent French. Everyone around her, including of course her friends and family, speaks only French and Arabic. She therefore has no difficulty integrating linguistically. After arriving in Quebec, she attended a francophone high school in Anjou. Yet a few years later, Djazia chose to stop living in French. When asked about that choice, she doesn’t mince words. “It’s not a language I have a lot of affinity with,” she confides. “Especially when my grandfather found out I was speaking French in Quebec, he was really angry.
Mon grand-père, c’est un Algérien. Il a: My grandfather is Algerian. He lived through the Algerian War, independence. It really affected him when he found out that we, here, were speaking French. During that time, I also started reading, which really opened my mind to the reality of France’s colonization of Algeria.” But it isn’t only Algeria’s colonial past that distances the young Montrealer from French. Her experience in the English-speaking world has been completely different from what she lived in francophone spheres, she says with emotion. She adds that she experienced more situations of exclusion at work and at school in francophone environments.
Selon elle, il existe une ouverture d’es: According to her, there is greater open-mindedness, sensitivity, academic support and understanding of the reality of immigrants in English-speaking environments in Quebec. At the end of high school, Djazia decided to leave the francophone system entirely. She headed to Dawson, an English-language CEGEP, then to Concordia, an English-language university. “The support you get is so great, especially when you come from a francophone school,” she says. “They ask you if you come from a francophone high school, and then you have services that are really available to you,” the young graduate reports.
Aujourd’hui, Djazia Bousnina pense que s: Today, Djazia Bousnina believes her postsecondary studies would have been very difficult had she done them in French. “I think I would have succeeded in my studies, because I’m an immigrant and we put a lot of pressure on ourselves, but I don’t think I would have enjoyed my path and I don’t think I would have dared to study politics.”
Djazia ne voit pas la nécessité de la lo: Djazia doesn’t see the need for Bill 96. For her, asking people who speak several languages to live in only one language, French, is utopian. The only consequence is to prevent people with diverse cultural backgrounds from flourishing in different cultures. “Imagine telling someone: ‘Stop being rich, become poorer.’ That’s what we’re asking of people. Stop being rich, become poorer! It’s crazy, because you would never say that to someone.
Mais l’État le demande, l’État efface de: But the State asks for it, the State erases people [...] it’s a cultural erasure, and we allow it because we don’t see culture as social capital. We see it as a social inconvenience.”
Djazia reconnaît que son rapport au fran: Djazia acknowledges that her relationship with French has evolved, notably thanks to some of her favourite authors, including Frantz Fanon and Ocean Vuong. She tells us that in the past she was adamant about not living in French, but today she has changed her mind. She now sees in French in Quebec a great decolonial power. “Many revolutionaries wrote in French and created a system of revolution, of challenges, a new dynamic in French. Now I’m reconsidering writing in French.”
Hany et Djazia, nous disent qu’ils aurai: Hany and Djazia tell us that they might have chosen to continue their studies in French had they received a better welcome in Quebec’s francophone system.
Teiawenhniseráhte Jeremy Tomlinson, dire: Teiawenhniseráhte Jeremy Tomlinson, director of the Kanesatake Health Centre. Photo: Fatima Bah
L’héritage colonial associé au français: The colonial legacy associated with French is also felt on Indigenous territories, where concerns about Bill 96 run very high. In Kahnawake and Kanesatake, several residents tell us they have other priorities than protecting French in Quebec, being more concerned with the aftermath of intergenerational trauma and the revitalization of Kanien’kéha, the Mohawk language. Exasperation with the French language and with Quebecers’ demands came up in every conversation we had with Indigenous people in the two reserves. All say the same thing: Indigenous languages are in peril. Protecting and revitalizing them are the priorities of Indigenous people, not speaking French, which for them is a colonial language. “How many times has someone said to me: ‘Speak French,’” says Teiawenhniseráhte Jeremy Tomlinson, director of the Kanesatake Health Centre. “To that, I often answer: ‘Technically, you’re on the territory of the Kanien’kehá:ka.
Tu es chanceux que je ne te demande pas: You’re lucky I’m not asking you to speak Mohawk.’” “French-speaking Quebecers are proud of their language,” says Jeff, an elder from the Kahnawake reserve who prefers not to give his full name. “Good for them. What about us? We’re proud of our language too. You don’t try to speak our language. Why do you want us to speak yours?” he asks. The Kahnawake band council has introduced Mohawk classes so young people can learn their traditional language in schools. The same initiative has been taken in the Mohawk territory of Kanesatake, where the number of people who speak Kanien’kéha keeps dropping. “Nine years ago, there were 150 people who spoke our language here in Kanesatake; today, there are fewer than 40 left,” laments Teiawenhniseráhte Jeremy Tomlinson. In the Kanesatake Health Centre, it’s hard not to notice the signs for the various departments.
Elles sont en trois langues : l’anglais,: They are in three languages: English, which appears first at the top of the signs, then Kanien’kéha just below, and finally French, at the bottom in smaller print. Elsewhere, a sign asks patients coming in to wash their hands, first in English, then in French and finally in Kanien’kéha. The health centre’s director isn’t afraid of having to change his signs to put French first. “They [the Quebec government] can try, but I’m not worried. I think there’s a line you don’t cross,” he answers. Even though the law provides exceptions for historically English-speaking communities like Kanesatake, the communities fear that these directives, which come from the highest levels, won’t necessarily be applied at the lowest levels of the hierarchy. Members of the English-speaking Indigenous communities we spoke with worry that Bill 96 will have certain perverse effects. “I’ve talked with several elders, and there’s a lot of stress, because they’re at a point in their lives when they need health care the most,” says Teiawenhniseráhte. Bill 96 requires that health care be provided in French, except in certain situations.
Il y a quelques semaines, dans la commun: A few weeks ago, in the Kanesatake community, an elder suffered a cardiac episode. He decided to go to the hospital in Hawkesbury, Ontario, about 45 minutes from the Mohawk territory, rather than the one in Saint-Eustache, a few minutes away. “It’s to get service in the language he understands and in which he feels most comfortable,” answers Jeremy Tomlinson when asked what drove the elder to travel so far. The elder had a heart attack in the hospital’s waiting room. Unable to revive him, the hospital transferred him to another institution, in Ottawa, where he ultimately died. Without saying that the elder died because of Bill 96, Teiawenhniseráhte believes the situation illustrates the apprehensions English-speaking Indigenous people have about francophone health services. And health isn’t the only area affected by this law.
Contrairement aux enfants de la loi 101,: Unlike the children covered by Bill 101, for whom spots are capped, English-speaking Indigenous students will be able to attend CEGEP in English without limits. Nevertheless, like all students in English-language CEGEPs, they will have to take three additional courses in French or of French instead of two courses in French. Teiawenhniseráhte fears that English-speaking Indigenous youth, who have a very high dropout rate, will have even more difficulty obtaining their college diploma because of this provision of Bill 96. In a spirit of reconciliation, he proposes instead that Indigenous students be accommodated and given the opportunity to learn Kanien’kéha to complete their college studies. In a context where efforts are being made to revitalize Indigenous languages and cultures, Jeremy Tomlinson fears that Bill 96 will reignite tensions between Indigenous and francophone communities.
Il cite le fait que les personnes autoch: He points to the fact that Indigenous people are rarely consulted on decisions that affect them daily to explain, among other things, the poor relations between the Quebec government and Indigenous peoples. The director of the Kanesatake Health Centre raises this while recalling the negative experience he had at the National Assembly of Quebec, where he went to debate Bill 96. “They gave me 15 minutes to speak, and by the time I started speaking, they cut into my speaking time because of technical problems.”
« Honnêtement, je pense que nous avons t: “Honestly, I think we have waited too long to have a real nation-to-nation meeting,” says the former chief of the Kanesatake band council. In his view, it is more than essential that his community’s interests be protected and that the government take them into account.
Lynn Delisle et Marlyn Kane, deux aînées: Lynn Delisle and Marlyn Kane, two elders from Kahnawake. Photo: Ramy Berkani

Lynn Delisle and Marlyn Kane, two elders from Kahnawake, never had the chance to learn to speak Kanien’kéha. They welcome us into their home to talk about their relationship with language. In Lynn’s garden, an anti–Bill 96 sign is displayed prominently. With the aim of protecting the French language in Quebec, the Act respecting French, the official and common language of Québec, pushes the population to learn and speak French. This takes Lynn Delisle and Marlyn Kane back to the era when attempts were made to assimilate Indigenous people. “Maybe we’re too sensitive to people imposing anything on us…” says Lynn Delisle, one of the founding mothers of Step by Step, Family and Child Centre in Kahnawake. Today, many initiatives are in place in Kahnawake to protect the Mohawk language. Lynn and Marlyn tell us they couldn’t benefit from that kind of initiative when they attended English-language school. “We’re almost like the sacrificed generation.
Bien que, parmi ces autres générations,: Although, among those other generations, some were punished for speaking their language,” Lynn Delisle tells us. Marlyn Kane agrees. The grandmothers explain that for them, language is an important part of their culture and builds a bridge to Indigenous youth. For them and for many Indigenous people in different communities, change has not always meant something good. “Speaking French would make our lives easier,” Lynn explains. “We’d have jobs. We’d have more influence over the Quebec government.”
Elle poursuit : « Les gens disent : “ No: She continues: “People say: ‘No, we’re not going to learn French. We’re not francophones.’ I look at them and I say: ‘We’re not anglophones either.’” As the conversation goes on, it becomes clear that what bothers her is rather the fact that Bill 96 imposes a language that isn’t theirs, once again. “That’s not a way to do things, and I see it so often that it’s never comforting… No one asks us where we stand with French, whether we need support with the French language and francophone culture. Imagine if they had come to us [Indigenous peoples] that way. They go to war instead of collaborating,” Lynn concludes.
La Converse a interrogé le bureau du min: La Converse asked the office of the minister responsible for the French language and francization, Simon Jolin-Barrette, about the concerns raised by our interviewees. Regarding fears about how the law will be applied in health and social services, the minister’s office replied that Bill 96 “is very clear on the question of health care” and that it will not prevent a citizen from being properly cared for, adding that an amendment had been added to reassure English-speaking Quebecers and that Bill 96 provides exceptions for health, safety, or when the principles of natural justice require it.
Le cabinet n’a cependant pas précisé com: The minister’s office did not specify, however, how it will ensure that the amendments are respected at every level. On the question of Indigenous languages, the minister’s office said it drafted Bill 96 in such a way that it “does not infringe on the right of First Nations and Inuit to maintain and develop their traditional languages and cultures,” while stating that “protecting the French language and protecting Indigenous languages are not in opposition.”
Le cabinet n’a pas indiqué s’il accorder: The office did not say whether or not it would grant an exemption to Indigenous students who want to learn their ancestral language. On the subject of newcomers, the office did not specify how it intends to accommodate people who cannot read and write or who have experienced trauma. The minister’s office instead reiterated that the six-month window Quebec has provided “for particular situations that would require the use of a language other than French does not represent a deadline for learning French,” adding that exceptions are provided and that immigrants will be served in French. No details were provided about the consequences for the migration process of newcomers who would not have mastered French at the end of that six-month period.
Enfin, à propos des préoccupations manif: Finally, regarding the concerns expressed by some racialized youth about francophone spaces, the office merely reiterated the law’s objective without specifying how it intends to address the feelings of exclusion these young people say they experience in francophone spaces.
Pendant des décennies, les Canadiens-fra: For decades, French Canadians were victims of discrimination. Until 1960, English-speaking men in Quebec earned much more and were more privileged than bilingual French-Canadian men. It took the Quiet Revolution of the 1960s for considerable socioeconomic changes to occur and improve the lot of Quebecers.
Depuis la Révolution tranquille, les gou: Since the Quiet Revolution, Quebec governments have worked to protect Quebec identity, notably by strengthening the French language. “The purpose of this bill is to affirm that the only official language of Quebec is French. It also affirms that French is the common language of the Quebec nation.” Those are the first words of Bill 96. In May 2021, the Legault government tabled the bill, which aims to “reduce the decline of the French language in the province.”
